title: NBC audition for the trio and the 1937-38 Aunt Jemima program
summary: The trio auditions at NBC without success, Hinton goes with Cab Calloway, and Levy later gets onto the Aunt Jemima program.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts

blocks.x: And he had tremendous. And then he was a student of it, too. And he had a fast ear and he picked up stuff that the trumpets would play and he'd slide his fingers on the strings, you know, and to the plane he'd slide it and he'd twist the strings, shove the strings in like you do on the banjo, see. Make a quarter tone, see. Yeah. And we did pretty good until, I don't know, I think the prohibition agents or something happened and they came in and we had to get another job. We went down and made an audition at NBC. And, oh, I'll tell you who came through Chicago. And, what's this lyric writer that wrote with, Andy, was it Andy Rezaff? Andy Rezaff? Andy Rezaff? Andy Rezaff. Andy Rezaff. Andy Rezaff. Yeah, he came through Chicago and he had a, he wanted to do a little thing on the radio, a little skit about musicians and a little numerous thing, a little bit on the art of Amos and Andy, but musicians came on. So he heard about our trio. So he came out the house and we did a rehearsal and he did some funny jive talk and we played. So it sounds so good. We went down to NBC and made an audition down there. And they, they owned up to it. It was awfully good. He came and congratulated us and said, gee, gee, and Wyatt really played some fiddle through double stops and harmonics and then all in swing, swing fiddle. You know, Joe Vanuja style, 80s style style. And so they said, well, we can't make up our minds. So Andy Rezaff, Andy Rezaff had a big name. You know, a lyric writer. We thought Joe was going to get on NBC. I did finally get on there with Sammy Williams' Aunt Jemima program in 1937. I was bandwagonist and guitarist on that program. The Pell player. Yes. He's tremendous. Fantastic memory and fantastic ear. I tell Nike, he brought a fellow up for me to take a song down. The fellow was singing in the cracks. And so Sammy said, he's singing near a D flat to be a singing C. That's a year, huh? Oh. So this thing with NBC, they liked it, but they couldn't make up their mind. You see, they had Amos Nandy and they didn't want anything to interfere with it. You see, that's what it was. See, what we should have did was take it over to CBS. So we made the audition. Audition was all right and everything. So that didn't pan out. So we jobbed on the north side with the little trio, my wife, Houston, myself, and Milt Hinton. And then I think Prohibition agents rated some places or something. And everything got tight. So Milt Hinton got a job with cab. He went with cab too. That's when he went with cab. And then I think I jobbed around and jobbed around. Finally this Angemiima thing came up. Sammy Williams got the Angemiima program. We were on then 37 and 38. That part of 37, first about six months, six, thirty-eight.
